source.title: Make the example corpora exemplars of good records

labels.name: Epic
labels.description: An umbrella issue holding a swimlane's detail, not a story to implement

source.body:
Adopters model their own records on the corpora under `examples/`. Comparing the engineering standards with
well-regarded public ones (Zalando's and Azure's API guidelines, Google's AIPs, OWASP ASVS, the GDS Way) found them
precise and short, with a traceable checklist, and found three faults in their shape:

* every rule is a MUST (135 in engineering, 0 SHOULD, 0 MAY), so a standard gives no latitude
* a reason sits in Rationale, not beside the rule
* no standard but one says how to depart from it

About a dozen rules also make a product or a mechanism mandatory where an outcome would do.

This epic makes the example corpora show what a good record of each type looks like, at the right level of detail, and
says why wherever they differ from good public practice. [Design intent](https://paul80nd.github.io/knowledge-as-code/framework/intent/)
states the direction.

Done when every type's worked examples have been compared with public exemplars, standards state MUST and SHOULD as
the intent page describes, and every type page states its level of detail and change cadence.

comments.text:
## The standards comparison, in full

This is the comparison #931 and #932 rest on, and the method #935 to #939 repeat for the other types. It was run on
2026-10-18 by reading five engineering standards whole (`std-API`, `std-OBS`, `std-DEPLOY`, `std-NETTST`,
`std-SECRET`) and `.schema/standards.yaml`, against public standards read from their primary sources.

### Method

1. Read our worked examples of the type whole, and the type's schema.
2. Read 4 to 6 well-regarded public examples of the same kind of document, from primary sources.
3. Measure the same things in each: keyword density and mix, how often a rule gives its reason, outcome against
   implementation, stated scope and exceptions, examples, length.
4. List findings by our record and clause id, each against the public practice it differs from, with a URL.
5. Say where ours are stronger, and recommend a shape: what to keep and what to change.

### Measurements

Our figures count only the `Rules` section. "Rules with a reason" is the share of keyword sentences carrying "because",
"so that", "so", "since", "to ensure" or "otherwise" in the same sentence. It undercounts Zalando and Azure, whose rules
each have a paragraph of explanation under them.

| Document | MUST per 1k words | MUST : SHOULD (: MAY) | Rules with a reason | Lean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ours, std-API | 19.5 | 12 : 0 | 8% | outcome in the rules, mechanism in headings and checklist |
| ours, std-OBS | 24.8 | 15 : 0 | 20% | outcome |
| ours, std-DEPLOY | 24.9 | 13 : 0 | 8% | outcome |
| ours, std-NETTST | 22.0 | 13 : 0 | 23% | implementation (named products, an exact command) |
| ours, std-SECRET | 15.0 | 8 : 0 | 0% | outcome |
| ours, all 12 engineering standards | 21.5 | 135 : 0 : 0 | about 10% | mixed |
| [Zalando RESTful API guidelines](https://opensource.zalando.com/restful-api-guidelines/) | 7.3 in capitals | 84 : 50 : 10 rule headings | 6%, every rule has a body | implementation |
| [Azure REST API guidelines](https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines/blob/vNext/azure/Guidelines.md) | 12.9 (DO / DO NOT) | 164 : 33 : 27 | 5%, with a body | implementation |
| [AIP-185](https://google.aip.dev/185) / [AIP-193](https://google.aip.dev/193) | 12.3 / 13.6 | 20 : 7 / 37 : 23 | 0 to 4% | implementation (formats) |
| [OWASP ASVS 5.0 V16](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/5.0/en/0x25-V16-Security-Logging-and-Error-Handling.md) | 17 requirements, levelled L2/L3 | none (latitude through levels) | 22% | outcome |
| [The GDS Way](https://github.com/alphagov/gds-way) (logging, monitoring, secrets) | about 1.5 | about 2 : 18, should-led | 15% | names tools, as recommendations |
| [The Twelve-Factor App](https://12factor.net/) (config, build-release-run, logs) | about 0 | principles only | prose reasons | outcome |

### Findings

1. **No latitude inside the document.** Every one of the 135 rules is a MUST, and only `std-GATES` mentions the
   deviation route. Azure defines SHOULD as "disclose your reason during review" and sends every exception to a named
   board. [AIP-200](https://google.aip.dev/200) makes a departure legitimate when it is annotated with a reason.
   Fixed in the type by #931; the records are #932.
2. **`std-API`'s checklist is stricter than its rule, and picks a contested mechanism.**
   `std-API.a-change-carries-a-version-and-a-notice` asks for "a version a consumer can pin to". The checklist requires
   a version segment in every path. Zalando rule 115 says MUST NOT use URL versioning, and rule 113 SHOULD avoid
   versioning. Azure uses an `api-version` query parameter; AIP-185 puts the major version in the path. Our MUST for
   `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers is a SHOULD in [Zalando rule 189](https://opensource.zalando.com/restful-api-guidelines/#189).
3. **`std-API.every-endpoint-authenticates-and-validates` contradicts itself.** "MUST authenticate the caller before it
   does any work" leaves no room for a health probe or a public read, yet its fourth bullet forbids serving personal
   data to an unauthenticated caller. Zalando rule 104 secures every endpoint but states the scheme in the OpenAPI
   document. The rule needs a stated scope.
4. **`std-API.the-contract-is-the-source-of-truth` over-reaches.** "A consumer MUST test against the published
   contract, not against a running instance" reads as a ban on integration testing against the provider. No public
   guide prescribes how a consumer tests. The rest of the rule is stronger than practice: Zalando's API-first rule 100
   asks for a specification, not for a build that fails on drift.
5. **`std-NETTST` makes products mandatory.** It requires xUnit, Testcontainers and `WebApplicationFactory` by name,
   names FluentAssertions as one of two permitted assertion styles, and fixes the exact coverage command. The GDS Way
   names tools as "we recommend". The xUnit reason ("one runner reports every suite") is weak: `dotnet test` runs NUnit
   and MSTest too. Unverified: that FluentAssertions moved to a commercial licence at version 8.
6. **`std-OBS.one-request-reads-as-one-timeline` is stricter than ASVS on time, and gives no reason.** We require UTC.
   ASVS 16.2.2 accepts UTC or an explicit offset, recommends UTC, and explains why. `std-OBS` is otherwise the best of
   the set: outcome-led, built on W3C Trace Context, and its alert rule is sharper than the GDS Way's.
7. **`std-DEPLOY` has no exceptions where practice needs them.** `std-DEPLOY.a-way-back-exists-before-the-change-goes`
   requires a migration to keep the previous version running, which some destructive changes cannot.
   `std-DEPLOY.production-changes-through-the-pipeline-alone` forbids every hand edit, with no break-glass route
   (unverified as industry norm). Elsewhere it matches Twelve-Factor III and V closely.
8. **Where ours are stronger.** Every rule traces to a policy clause on a `Covers` line. Every standard has a testable
   checklist, which only ASVS matches. Every example says why the avoided form fails. At about 520 to 615 words, each is
   a fraction of an AIP's 1,600 to 2,700. The weakness is that reasons sit in Rationale, not beside the rule; Zalando
   and Azure put a short paragraph under every rule.

### Recommended shape

Keep: one rule group per heading, capitals-only BCP 14 keywords, `Covers:`, Good and Avoid examples with their why, the
conformance checklist, the short length.

Change: MUST for the outcome and SHOULD for the mechanism, with an "unless"; a fixed line to the deviation route; one
short "because" where the reason is not obvious; a stated scope or exception on the authentication, migration and
hand-edit rules; a checklist that tests only what the rules require. #931 put the first three into the type.

comments.text:
## The policies and ADRs comparison, in full

This is the comparison behind #935. It was run on 2026-10-18 by reading the 24 engineering policies and `adr-0001`
whole, with their schemas and type pages, against public examples read from their primary sources.

### Method

1. Read our worked examples of the type whole, and the type's schema.
2. Read 6 well-regarded public examples of the same kind of document, from primary sources, and count real ADRs from
   three public repositories.
3. Measure the same things in each. For policies: the modal mix, rows with a reason, outcome against mechanism,
   figures, scope and exceptions, length, review cadence and ownership. For ADRs: the sections, the length, how
   alternatives and consequences are given, the status lifecycle and immutability.
4. List findings by record and clause id, each against the public practice it differs from, with a URL.
5. Say where ours are stronger, and recommend a shape.

### Policies: measurements

"Reason" means the same clause row contains so, so that, because, since, otherwise or to ensure.

| Document | Words | Binding : should : may/could | Rows with a reason | Figures in clauses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ours, 24 engineering policies | 325 to 917 | 237 : 28 : 11 (86% binding) | 22 of 276 (8%); every Purpose argues the position | 7 clauses |
| [SANS Access Management](https://www.sans.org/information-security-policy/) | 668 | 13 "shall" : 0 : 0 | 0 of 13, reason in Purpose | none, kept in a separate standard |
| [GovS 007 Security](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/613a195bd3bf7f05b694d647/GovS_007-_Security.pdf) | about 8,900 | 49 : 106 : 8, terms defined | about 12% | none |
| [NCSC CAF B2](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/cyber-assessment-framework/caf-objective-b/principle-b2-identity-and-access-control) | about 2,000 | outcomes, no modals | about 11%, in a description | graded by level |
| [NIST SP 800-53 AC-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/usnistgov/oscal-content/main/nist.gov/SP800-53/rev5/json/NIST_SP-800-53_rev5_catalog.json) | about 330 | imperatives | 0, reason in Discussion | an organisation-defined parameter |
| [GitLab Access Management](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/security/security-and-technology-policies/access-management-policy/) | 256 | present tense, no modals | 0 of 7 | none, kept in a linked standard |
| [GDS Technology Code of Practice](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-technology-code-of-practice) | 641 | 3 : 3 : 0 | about 3 of 13 | none |

### Policies: findings

1. **`pol-MEXP.PRIVATE` read "MUST prefer private paths".** A preference is a recommendation, and GovS 007 defines
   should as one. Fixed: it is now a SHOULD.
2. **`pol-TRUS.PINNED` said how** ("keep the exact versions… in version control"). CAF and SANS state outcomes. Fixed:
   "**MUST** make two builds of the same source resolve the same component versions".
3. **Seven clauses carry a figure:** `pol-VURM.TIMEBOX`, `pol-OBSV.AUDIT`, `pol-RECV.RESTORE`, `pol-RECV.PROVEN`,
   `pol-INCR.WINDOW`, `pol-ACCS.VALID` and `pol-ACCS.RECERT`. SANS and GitLab put figures in a standard, and NIST makes
   the figure a parameter. Deliberate difference, stated on `policies.md` and in the lineage: a figure is the limit the
   owner accepts, and a standard may only tighten it. `std-DEPS` already does: 7 days for a critical finding, against
   TIMEBOX's 14.
4. **COULD where public documents use may.** GovS 007 says "may denotes approval". Deliberate difference, stated in the
   same two places: COULD states an aspiration, and MAY grants a permission, which a policy has no use for.
5. **No roles section and no approval record.** NIST AC-1 and GitLab ask for roles and responsibilities, and GovS 007
   and GitLab record approval. Deliberate difference: the `owner` answers for a policy, and the reviewed pull request
   that sets `status: active` is its approval.
6. **All 24 policies are `draft`.** The policy-lookup skill presents a draft clause as a proposal. They stay draft,
   because the corpus goes to an adopting organisation, which approves each one in its own name. `policies.md` says a
   policy becomes `active` on the day its owner approves it, and the engineering README says the policies await that.
7. **Review cadence and length match.** Every policy is reviewed annually and earlier when the estate, the law or a
   framework changes, matching NIST's "[frequency] and following [events]". The median length is about 490 words.

### ADRs: measurements

| Source | Length | Alternatives | Consequences | Statuses | Edits after acceptance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ours, adr-0001 before the change | 1,192 to 1,306 words | required, each with a verdict, checked | 8 to 9 bullets, gains and costs mixed | MADR's five, with `rejected` | status, typo, link, and "a sentence that no longer matches the decision" |
| [Nygard](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions) | "one or two pages" | none | "positive, negative, and neutral" | four, no rejected | keep the old one, mark it superseded |
| [MADR 4](https://adr.github.io/madr/) | not stated | Considered Options required; pros and cons optional | optional, Good / Bad | five, with rejected | not stated |
| [Henderson](https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/architecture-decision-record) | not stated | under Rationale | review after one month | lifecycle stages | immutable in theory; dated additions in practice |
| [AWS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/architectural-decision-records/adr-process.html) | example about 250 words | not required | Positive / Negative | Rejected, with a reason | immutable once accepted or rejected |
| [GDS Way](https://gds-way.digital.cabinet-office.gov.uk/standards/architecture-decisions.html) | not stated | not required | positive and negative | the PR state stands for the status | clarifications in place; a new ADR once implemented |
| [Azure Well-Architected](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/well-architected/architect-role/architecture-decision-record) | "pithy" | options, including those ruled out | "avoid hiding consequences" | Proposed / Accepted / Superseded | "append-only log. Don't go back and edit accepted records" |
| real ADRs: alphagov/govuk-aws, alphagov/govuk-infrastructure, backstage (80 files) | medians 216, 440 and 289 words | 1 file in 80 has the section | | | |

### ADRs: findings

1. **`adr-0001` ran about three times the real median**, against our own "a few narrative paragraphs". Fixed:
   `adrs.md` asks for about a page, and the template seed is cut to about 600 words. The two accepted copies were
   brought down to match as a stated one-off exception, because they are worked examples with no consumer. Their
   decision, alternatives and verdicts are unchanged. The seed's note to the adopter moved to an HTML comment, so the
   exported Context opens on the problem.
2. **The in-place edit was unbounded.** #615 changed an alternative's verdict after acceptance, through "a sentence that
   no longer matches the decision". Fixed: `adrs.md` allows only "a correction that leaves the decision, its
   alternatives and their verdicts as agreed". `contributing.md` and `shaping-a-type.md` now agree with it.
3. **Six decisions under one id.** Henderson asks for one decision per ADR, and Azure splits a decision by phase. No
   change: the trimmed copies state the approach in three bullets.
4. **Consequences** pair each cost with what it buys, where MADR and AWS split Good and Bad. Deliberate difference.
5. **Confidence and a trigger to revisit** (Azure, MADR) are written inline where they matter. No new field.

### Where ours are stronger

- **Policies:** a stable clause id the tool resolves; per-clause framework alignment, rolled up and checked; an
  exceptions route through `pol-DEVI` as complete as GitLab's, which also lists the clauses no deviation can touch; scope
  on every policy, and boundary lines between sibling policies, which none of the exemplars has.
- **ADRs:** the Y-statement, which only Zimmermann has; a verdict on every alternative, checked by the tool; supersession
  recorded as a pair of fields checked in both directions; `decided-on` and `deciders` as fields.

### Recommended shape

- **Policies.** Keep Purpose, Scope, Clauses and Exceptions, outcome-led MUST with SHOULD and COULD, reasons in Purpose,
  boundary lines, the `pol-DEVI` route and an annual review. A clause states the outcome, and the type page states why
  figures, COULD and approval by PR differ from public practice.
- **ADRs.** Keep the sections, the Y-statement, alternatives with verdicts, five statuses and supersession fields.
  About a page, and an edit in place only for a correction that leaves the decision as agreed.

### Not verified

ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clause 5.2 and A.5.1 (paywalled), the legacy SANS template layout (no longer published), what MADR
says about immutability, the gov.uk "ADR-000" template, and whether GovS 007 has an edition later than v2.0.

`pol-INCR`'s note explaining away `WINDOW` against `HARM` is filed as #962.

## The processes, runbooks and fixes comparison, in full

This is the comparison behind #936. It was run on 2026-10-18 by reading the 9 dog-fooding processes, the 3 dog-fooding
runbooks and the 3 fixes (two in dog-fooding, one in payments) whole, with their schemas, type pages and template seeds,
against public examples read from their primary sources. The Google and PagerDuty quotes came through a page
summariser.

### Method

1. Read our worked examples of each type whole, with the type's schema and seed, and check each quoted command and
   message against the code.
2. Read 4 to 5 public examples of each kind of document from primary sources.
3. Measure the same things in each. Runbooks: step granularity, the expected result per step, escalation,
   prerequisites, rollback, length, rehearsal. Fixes: a symptom-first title, environment, cause, verification, reuse.
   Processes: step level, roles, inputs and outputs, length, departures.
4. List findings by record id, each against the public practice it differs from, with a URL.
5. Say where ours are stronger, and recommend a shape. For runbooks, a fresh agent then walked the edited records.

### Runbooks: measurements

| Source | Steps | Expected result per step | Escalation | Prerequisites | Rollback | Words | Rehearsal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ours, 3 runbooks | numbered, one command each | 3 of 17 resolution steps, plus `Confirmed when` | when, who and how; timed only in nuget-404 | `requires-tools`, `requires-access` | none stated | 556 to 657 | a dated field, all `"never"` |
| [Google SRE](https://sre.google/sre-book/being-on-call/) and [Workbook](https://sre.google/workbook/on-call/) | "high-level instructions"; automate a list of commands | not addressed | "clear escalation paths" | not stated | rollback must be tested | n/a | Wheel of Misfortune, DiRT; no date |
| [PagerDuty](https://response.pagerduty.com/during/during_an_incident/) | by role, 3–7 prose steps | none | timed, 5 minutes | not stated | not stated | about 1,300 | "constantly tested" |
| [GitLab runbooks](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-com/runbooks) | prose to command blocks | "expect RUNNING" in the best one | named roles plus a timebox | "Use this when", "Before you start" | optional Rollback; failure branches inline | 334 to 2,739 | a prose note; no date |
| [AWS OPS07-BP03](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/operational-excellence-pillar/ops_ready_to_support_use_runbooks.html) | "a checklist" | none; someone else runs it | Escalation POC field | tools and permissions | error handling | n/a | owner; change management |

### Runbooks: findings

1. **`rbk-goldens-disagree` regenerated more than it said, and did not match how the suite reports a failure.** The
   golden filter is a substring match, so `--update export` also regenerates `export-inherited` and `export-policies`.
   Fixed: the page says so, and asks the reader to check every `UPDATE` line for `WARNING`, because `--update` exits 0
   with one. It describes a failure as a line opening `FAIL` with indented detail, and asks about a dropped export path
   before anything can regenerate it. A CI-only failure fetches `origin/main` and reruns the unit layer with
   `KAC_BASE_REF` before it escalates.
2. **`rbk-goldens-disagree` reproduced a failure without CI's environment.** Fixed: it runs the suite with
   `GITHUB_ACTIONS=true`.
3. **`rbk-restore-cannot-find-version` passed a stale lock locally and left the working directory ambiguous.**
   `restore` skips a consumer whose `.imports/` already has the locked version. Fixed: the immediate actions delete
   `.imports/`, repack the producer and restore, as CI does. Every command names its directory. Two more refusal
   messages became symptoms with their own branches, and the lock is compared with the producer's `content-version` in
   both directions.
4. **Few steps said what the reader sees.** `runbooks.md` asks for it, and GitLab does it. Fixed: every step that prints
   something states its output, taken from a real run.
5. **No step said how to undo it.** GitLab has an optional Rollback and Google tests rollback. Fixed with one line per
   state-changing step inside Resolution, and no schema change.
6. **The runbooks had never been rehearsed.** No exemplar dates a rehearsal, so the field is ours. A tabletop walk of
   `rbk-goldens-disagree` and `rbk-restore-cannot-find-version`, by an agent that had not written them, found that
   neither could be followed as written. Both were fixed and dated 2026-10-18. `rbk-nuget-404-on-publish` stays
   `"never"` until a release.
7. **Library's runbook template carried Diagnosis guidance from before #787.** Fixed by copying the seed's lines across.
8. **Untimed escalation, and no alert linking to a runbook.** Deliberate difference: these are sev3 with one
   maintainer, and `dev-no-incident-process` accepts the departure from `eng:pol-INCR`.
9. **A deterministic list of commands is a candidate for automation.** Deliberate difference, already stated in the
   runbook lineage: the type stays a document.

### Fixes: measurements

| Source | Symptom title | Environment | Cause | Verification | Reuse tracked | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ours, 3 fixes | 3 of 3, paraphrased | 3 of 3; fix-0002 had no version | required | each ends on a check step | `review-by` plus `verified` | 324 to 390 |
| [KCS v6](https://library.serviceinnovation.org/KCS/KCS_v6/KCS_v6_Practices_Guide/030/030/020/010) | "requestor's words" | required, "precise" | optional | Validated by the requestor | case link, reuse count; "reuse is review" | no rule |
| [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/system-management-components/error-event-1601-click-roles-server-manager) | action plus "error message" | "Applies to" | 2 sentences | none | page feedback | about 550 |
| [Red Hat 31453](https://access.redhat.com/solutions/31453) | the log line, verbatim | versions plus a condition | gated | "Solution Verified" | not visible | about 80 public |
| [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/troubleshooting-ssh/error-permission-denied-publickey) | the error, verbatim | tabs per operating system | 1 line | "You should see" per check | none | about 1,170 |

### Fixes: findings

1. **`fix-0002` named no version.** Fixed: "Rider 2026.2 on macOS 26", re-verified by its owner. `fixes.md` step 4 and the
   template ask for the versions a fix is known to apply to, at the precision that changes the answer, with a build
   number only where the behaviour depends on it.
2. **Nothing tracked reuse.** Fixed by adopting KCS's "reuse is review": a reader who applies a fix and sees it work adds
   or moves their `verified` entry. Deliberate difference, stated in the lineage: KCS counts uses and we do not, and
   `review-by` also dates a fix nobody reuses.
3. **Titles paraphrase the error**, with the literal text in `symptom-keywords`. Deliberate difference, already stated on
   the type page.
4. **Verification and lifecycle are stronger.** Every fix ends on a check step, and `verified` names who checked, where
   KCS and Red Hat show only a state.

### Processes: measurements

| Source | Step level | Roles | Inputs and outputs | Words | Departure |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ours, 9 processes | 5–14 outcomes (#934) | `owner` only | When to use, Prerequisites, Verification, "Close by stating" | 501 to 1,233 | `Optional:` on 4 steps in 1 record |
| [GOV.UK assessment](https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/service-assessments/how-service-assessments-work) | task level, links out | panel roles | entry test; exit graded red, amber or green | about 2,000 | named exemptions |
| [GitLab Change Management](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/infrastructure-platforms/change-management/) | task level, issue templates | roles table | "does my change need one" | about 4,900 | exceptions tracked and approved |
| [GitLab Handbook Usage](https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/about/handbook-usage/) | change by merge request; cross-link | CODEOWNERS | problem, MR, announce | about 5,000 | "responsibility over rigidity" |
| [ISO 9001 guidance](https://ma.iaqg.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/ISO9001_2015_Guidance_on_Documented_Information.docx) | scales with competence | 4.4.1 responsibilities | 4.4.1 inputs and outputs | about 1,740 | audited against the clause |

### Processes: findings

Not edited here, while `trials/process-level/` measures the pilot. They are on #960: `processes.md` contradicts its own
level, the departure route lives outside the records, the type has no roles, and some entry tests and access entries are
missing. The exemplars agree with #934's outcome level and contradict none of its verdicts.

### Where ours are stronger

- **Runbooks:** a checked `Symptoms`-first order, `Confirmed when` with a route to escalation, symptom-named titles, a
  dated rehearsal with a method, and a length at the short end of GitLab's real range.
- **Fixes:** a named verifier, with a trust level derived from the list.
- **Processes:** an exported `When to use this` and `Prerequisites`, and a dated walk-through.

### Recommended shape

- **Runbooks.** Keep the sections, checks and fields. Each step states what the reader sees and how to undo it, names
  its directory, reproduces the failure the way CI sees it before diagnosing it, and is walked and dated.
- **Fixes.** Keep Symptom, Environment, Cause and Resolution, `How we found it`, `symptom-keywords` and `verified`. Give
  versions at the precision that changes the answer, and record a reuse in `verified`.

### Not verified

ITIL 4 known-error wording (secondary sources only), Red Hat's gated sections, the text of ISO 9001 clauses 4.4.1 and
7.5.2, word-exact Google and PagerDuty quotes, PagerDuty's runbook template page, AWS OPS07-BP04 and OPS10-BP02, and the
Wikimedia and Atlassian runbooks.

## The services, data, integrations, offerings and tools comparison, in full

This is the comparison behind #937. It was run on 2026-10-18 by reading the 15 services (dog-fooding, library, payments),
4 data records, 5 integrations, 5 offerings (library, payments) and 14 tools (dog-fooding) whole, with their schemas,
lineage, type pages and template seeds, against public examples read from their primary sources. Every tool's
`packages` range was checked against the real manifests, and the dog-fooding service facts against the workflows.

### Method

1. Read our worked examples of each type whole, with the schema, the lineage, the type page and the seed.
2. Check each record against the estate it describes: the package pins, the workflows, the CLI's verbs.
3. Read 4 to 6 public examples per type or group, from primary sources.
4. Measure the same things in each: fields, ownership, lifecycle and tier, relationships, links to live systems, length,
   and how drift is caught.
5. List findings by record id, each against the public practice it differs from, with a URL.
6. Say where ours are stronger, and recommend a shape.

### Services: measurements

### Tools: findings

1. **`tol-spectre-console` approved `Spectre.Console.Cli` 0.55.x, and the project referenced 0.57.2 since Dependabot's
   #802**, which carried no new assessment although `std-A11Y` asks for one at a new minor. Fixed: the range is 0.57.x,
   and the assessment was repeated by reading every call that colours or prompts at 0.57.2. It found one claim wrong:
   the browsing address `new` asks for has no flag of its own, and `--yes` derives it from the git remote. The record
   now says so. This is the drift `drift-against-manifests` would catch (#15).
2. **`tol-dotnet-sdk` called .NET the runtime of every tool in the register.** Fixed: the register's NuGet packages.
3. **The lineage quoted the Radar's `hold`.** Thoughtworks renamed it Caution. Fixed.
4. **CycloneDX and SPDX name a supplier.** Deliberate, now stated in the tools lineage: the register approves packages
   and is no software bill of materials, so `homepage` reaches the maintainer.
5. **11 of 13 entries record no alternative, and the register has no `trial` or `rejected` entry.** A gap, left open:
   no evaluation was invented.
6. **Eight GitHub Actions the workflows use have no entry.** Filed as #965.

### Where ours are stronger

- **Services:** `criticality` checked across dependency edges, `monitoring-output` as a commitment, "Taken from" source
  lines, and open questions written down. Backstage has no tier.
- **Data:** `review-by` with a warning, where no exemplar has a review date; retention in practice against policy;
  where each recipient processes the data.
- **Integrations:** checked fallbacks, `Exit` and `Commercials`, which neither API spec nor Backstage has.
- **Offerings:** verb-led task titles and a checked hub ratio.
- **Tools:** concluded and declared licences apart, `rejected` as a stance, a range for new work, and a review date.

### Recommended shape

- **Services.** Keep the document, `criticality`, `monitoring-output` and the sourcing lines. Link every data and
  integration record the prose names.
- **Data.** Keep it per domain, with `review-by` and practice against policy.
- **Integrations.** Keep the sections. `Contract` points at the published API description.
- **Offerings.** Unchanged. Known limitations states limitations, not status.
- **Tools.** Keep the fields. Move a `packages` range in the change that moves the manifest, until #15 automates it.
